nodes.name: Easy part of Conjecture 6.1
nodes.statement:
As evidence towards Conjecture~\ref{conj:weak}, we point out that the ``easy part'' of the conjecture follows from the Nash-Williams--Tutte theorem.
One can check that, even in general hypergraphs, every tree-assignment of a $k$-weakly-partition-connected hypergraph gives a $k$-partition connected graph.
Thus, any tree-assignment graph can be partitioned into $k$ spanning trees by the Nash-Williams--Tutte theorem, establishing the ``existence'' part of the graph $G$ being $k$-distinguishable.
Thus, the hard part of Conjecture~\ref{conj:weak} is the ``uniqueness'' part, finding a spanning tree partition with a unique signature.
nodes.statement_short: Every tree-assignment of a $k$-weakly-partition-connected hypergraph has $k$ spanning trees; only the unique-signature part is hard.

nodes.name: Relaxed hypergraph Nash-Williams--Tutte theorem

  Every $C(\log t)k$-weakly-partition-connected hypergraph $H$ on $t$ vertices has a tree-assignment with a $k$-distinguishable subgraph.

conclusions: Every $C(\log t)k$-weakly-partition-connected hypergraph $H$ on $t$ vertices has a tree-assignment with a $k$-distinguishable subgraph.

nodes.name: Derivation of Theorem 6.4 from CS07 and CCV09
nodes.statement:
The results in \cite{CS07,CCV09} look slightly different from Theorem~\ref{thm:conj-weak} and we briefly describe the connection here.
Both of the works prove that every $C(\log t)k$-weakly partition-connected hypergraph has $k$ hyperedge-disjoint connected subhypergraphs:\footnote{A hypergraph is connected if, for every two vertices $v$ and $v'$, there is a path $v=v_0,v_1,\dots,v_\ell=v'$ such that, for all $i$, $v_{i-1},v_i$ share a hyperedge.}
the first \cite{CS07} proves an equivalent statement about bipartite Steiner tree packings, and the second \cite{CCV09} proves a more general result about disjoint bases of polymatroids and also improves the constant $C$ in front of the log factor over \cite{CS07}.
Furthermore, it is not difficult to show that, for any hypergraph $H$ with $k$ hyperedge-disjoint connected subhypergraphs $H_0,\dots,H_{k-1}$, any tree assignment of $H$ has a $k$-distinguishable subgraph: briefly, the $k$-distinguishable subgraph $G$ is the union of spanning trees $T_0,\dots,T_{k-1}$ of the tree assignments of $H_0,\dots,H_{k-1}$ that are implied by the tree assignments of $H$, and the spanning trees $T_0,\dots,T_{k-1}$ give the $k$ edge-disjoint spanning trees of $G$ that certify $k$-distinguishability.
Hence, any $C(\log t)k$-weakly-partition-connected hypergraph has $k$ hyperedge-disjoint connected subhypergraphs and thus is $k$-distinguishable, which is Theorem~\ref{thm:conj-weak}.
nodes.statement_short: Hyperedge-disjoint connected subhypergraphs from CS07/CCV09 yield spanning trees certifying $k$-distinguishability.

nodes.name: Second proof of Theorem 1.1 (sketch)
nodes.statement:
We point out that Theorem~\ref{thm:conj-weak} can be used to obtain a second proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main-LD} by following the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:complete-2}, which connects hypergraph partitions to intersection matrices and then applies a polynomial method to obtain list decodable Reed--Solomon codes.
The extra $O(\log t)$ factor in the weak-partition-connectivity of Theorem~\ref{thm:conj-weak} appears as an $O(\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon})$ factor loss in the rate of the Reed--Solomon code.
Since one proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main-LD} is already given, and the key ideas for this second proof are covered throughout the rest of the paper, we omit the details of this second proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main-LD}.
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: Theorem 6.4 plus the intersection-matrix argument of Theorem 6.2 and the polynomial method, losing $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ in rate.

nodes.name: Linear independence of B_t
nodes.statement: \black{Note that $\mathcal{B}_t$ is formed by the set of vectors representing the oriented triangles $\Delta_{ijt}$ with the third vertex fixed to $t$.} The vectors in $\mathcal{B}_t$  are linearly independent since  $u^{\Delta_{ijt}}_{\{i,j\}}=1$ and $u^{\Delta_{ijt}}_{\{i',j'\}}=0$ for $1\leq i<j\leq t-1$ and  $1\leq i'<j'\leq t-1$ with $\{i,j\}\neq \{i',j'\}$.
nodes.statement_short: The triangle vectors are linearly independent via private coordinates.

nodes.name: Reduction to spanning
nodes.statement:
Let $W$ be the span of $\mathcal{B}_t$ over $\mathbb{F}$.
Consider an arbitrary oriented cycle $C$ in $K_t$. We claim that $u^C\in W$, and this would imply that $\mathcal{B}_t$ is a basis of \black{the cycle space} $C(K_t)$ and that the dimension of $C(K_t)$ is $|\mathcal{B}_t|=\binom{t-1}{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to showing every oriented cycle vector lies in the span $W$.

nodes.name: Induction setup and base
nodes.statement:
Denote by $e_C$ the smallest $\{i,j\}\in \binom{[t]}{2}$ in the lexicographic order such that $(i,j)\in C$ or $(j,i)\in C$.
Next, we will prove the claim by a reverse induction on the lexicographic order of $e_C$. Note that $t\not\in e_C$ since $|C|\geq 3$, which implies that the claim is vacuously true when $e_C=\{t-1,t\}$ (which never occurs).
nodes.statement_short: Set up reverse induction on the smallest edge $e_C$; base case vacuous.

nodes.name: Inductive hypothesis
nodes.statement:
Now assume that the claim holds for all oriented cycles $C'$ with $e_{C'}> e_{C}$.
Let $\{i,j\}=e_C$, where $i<j$.
We may assume that $(i,j)\in C$ by flipping the orientation of $C$ if necessary, which corresponds to negating  $u^C$.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive hypothesis; orient $C$ so that $(i,j)\in C$.

nodes.name: Subtract triangle
nodes.statement:
Let $s$ be the number of directed edges  that $C$ and $\Delta_{ijt}$ share. If $s=3$ then it is clear by definition that
$C=\Delta_{ijt}$, and we are done. Otherwise, $1\leq s\leq 2$ and it is easy to verify \black{by a case analysis} that $u^C-u^{\Delta_{ijt}}=u^{C'}$ for a set $C'$ that is either an oriented cycle in $G$ or a disjoint union of two oriented cycles $C_1, C_2$ in $G$ passing through $t$. The latter case occurs when \black{$s=1$, $C$ passes through $t$, and $\{(t,i),(j,t)\}\cap C=\emptyset$}. \black{As $C'$ is obtained from $C$ by removing its smallest edge $(i,j)$ (under the lexicographic order) and adding one (when $s=2$) or two (when $s=1$) edges greater $(i,j)$,} in either case, the smallest edge of $C'$  is greater than the edge $e_C=\{i,j\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Subtract $\Delta_{ijt}$; by cases on shared edges, the remainder has a larger smallest edge.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence, by the induction hypothesis and the fact that $u^{C'}=u^{C_1}+u^{C_2}$ when $C'$ is the disjoint union of $C_1$ and $C_2$, we have $u^{C'}\in W$. So $u^C=u^{C'}+u^{\Delta_{ijt}}\in W$, completing the proof of the claim.
nodes.statement_short: By induction $u^{C'}\in W$, so $u^C\in W$.

nodes.name: Inclusion-exclusion
nodes.statement:
By \eqref{definition-weight} (the definition of weight) and the inclusion-exclusion principle \begin{equation} {{\rm wt}}(I_{[t]})=\sum_{i=1}^t|I_i|-\left|\bigcup_{i=1}^tI_i\right|=\sum_{j=2}^t\sum_{J\in\binom{[t]}{j}}(-1)^{|J|}\left|\bigcap_{i\in J}I_i\right|.
\end{equation}
nodes.section: 3 Connection to Tree Packing and an Intermediate Result
nodes.statement_short: Inclusion-exclusion for the weight.

nodes.name: Matrix is square
nodes.statement:
Therefore, by assumption (i) of Theorem \ref{theorem-weaker} we have ${\rm wt}(I_{[t]})=\sum_{1\le i<j\le t} |I_i\cap I_j|$. Then, by assumption (iii)
the  matrix $M_{k,(I_1,\ldots,I_t)}$ is in fact a square matrix of order $\binom{t}{2}k$.
nodes.section: 3 Connection to Tree Packing and an Intermediate Result
nodes.statement_short: Empty triple intersections and (iii) make $M$ square.

nodes.name: Conclude for subsets
nodes.statement: Similarly, \eqref{constraint-weaker} holds for any $J\subseteq [t]$ with $|J|\ge 2$.
nodes.section: 3 Connection to Tree Packing and an Intermediate Result
nodes.statement_short: The same computation gives (5) for every $J$.

nodes.name: Fix partition
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{P}=\{V_1,\ldots,V_s\}$ be an arbitrary partition of $V$. Then it is clear that $\sum_{i=1}^s |V_i|=t$.
nodes.section: 3 Connection to Tree Packing and an Intermediate Result
nodes.statement_short: Fix an arbitrary partition.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: According to Lemma \ref{Nash-Williams}, to prove the claim it suffices to show that $G$ has at least $(s-1)k$ cross-edges with respect to $\mathcal{P}$.
nodes.section: 3 Connection to Tree Packing and an Intermediate Result
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to counting cross-edges via Nash-Williams--Tutte.

nodes.name: Total edges
nodes.statement: By \eqref{constraint-weaker} and assumption (iii) of Theorem \ref{theorem-weaker} it is easy to see that $G$ contains $\sum_{1\le i<j\le t}|I_i\cap I_j|=(t-1)k$ edges.
nodes.section: 3 Connection to Tree Packing and an Intermediate Result
nodes.statement_short: $G$ has $(t-1)k$ edges.

nodes.name: Edges inside parts
nodes.statement: Moreover, by \eqref{constraint-weaker} and assumption (ii) of Theorem \ref{theorem-weaker} one can infer that for each $i\in[s]$, the induced subgraph of $G$ on the vertex set $V_i$ has at most ${\rm wt}(I_j:j\in V_i)\le (|V_i|-1)k$ edges.
nodes.section: 3 Connection to Tree Packing and an Intermediate Result
nodes.statement_short: Each part induces at most $(|V_i|-1)k$ edges.

nodes.name: Count cross-edges
nodes.statement:
It follows that the number of cross-edges of $G$ (with respect to $\mathcal{P}$) is at least
$$
(t-1)k-\sum_{i=1}^s (|V_i|-1)k=\left(t-1-\sum_{i=1}^s |V_i|+s\right)k=(s-1)k,
$$
as needed, thereby completing the proof of the claim.
nodes.section: 3 Connection to Tree Packing and an Intermediate Result
nodes.statement_short: Subtract to get at least $(s-1)k$ cross-edges.

nodes.name: If direction
nodes.statement:
First we prove the if direction.
Assume to the contrary that we can remove from  $\mathcal{B}_t$ some columns labeled by an acyclic subgraph $H$ of $K_t$ and reduce the row rank.
Let $\mathcal{B}'_t$ be the submatrix of $\mathcal{B}_t$ after the removal of the columns labeled by  $H$. The rows of   $\mathcal{B}'_t$ are linearly dependent by assumption. Hence, there exists a nonzero vector $u\in\mathbb{F}^{\binom{t-1}{2}}$ such that $u\cdot\mathcal{B}'_t=0$. As $u\neq 0$ and the rows of $\mathcal{B}_t$ are linearly independent, we have $u\cdot\mathcal{B}_t\neq 0$. Let $S\subseteq \binom{[t]}{2}$ be the support of $u\cdot\mathcal{B}_t$, where the support of a vector of length $n$ is the subset of $[n]$ that records the indices of its nonzero coordinates. As $u\cdot\mathcal{B}_t\neq 0$ and $u\cdot\mathcal{B}'_t=0$, we have $\emptyset\neq S\subseteq H$.

Consider the  $\binom{t}{2}\times t$ matrix $D=(D_{\{i,j\},s})$
which is defined   by
\[
D_{\{i,j\},s}=\begin{cases}
1 & s=j, \\
-1 & s=i, \\
0 & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\]
where  $1\leq i<j\leq t \text{ and } s\in [t]$. Note that the rows and columns of $D$ are  labeled by $\{i,j\}\in \binom{[t]}{2}$
and  $s\in [t]$ respectively. It is not hard to check that $\mathcal{B}_t\cdot D=0$. \black{Indeed, for $1\le i<j\le t-1$ and $1\le s\le t$, let us compute the inner product of the $\{i,j\}$-th row of $\mathcal{B}_t$, i.e. $u^{\Delta_{ijt}}$, and the $s$-th column of $D$, denoted by $D^s$. As $u^{\Delta_{ijt}}$ has only three nonzero coordinates: $u^{\Delta_{ijt}}_{\{i,j\}}=1,~u^{\Delta_{ijt}}_{\{i,t\}}=-1$, and $u^{\Delta_{ijt}}_{\{j,t\}}=1$, by the definition of $D$ one can observe that
\begin{itemize}
    \item [(i)] if $s\not\in\{i,j,t\}$ then $D^s_{\{i,j\}}=D^s_{\{i,t\}}=D^s_{\{j,t\}}=0$;
    \item [(ii)] if $s=i$ then $D^s_{\{i,j\}}=D^s_{\{i,t\}}=-1,~D^s_{\{j,t\}}=0$;
    \item [(iii)]  if $s=j$ then $D^s_{\{i,j\}}=1,~D^s_{\{i,t\}}=0,~D^s_{\{j,t\}}=-1$;
    \item [(iv)] if $s=t$ then $D^s_{\{i,j\}}=0,~D^s_{\{i,t\}}=D^s_{\{j,t\}}=1$.
\end{itemize}
One can check that in all of the four cases listed above, the inner product $u^{\Delta_{ijt}}\cdot D^s=0$, which implies that $\mathcal{B}_t\cdot D=0$ and hence $u\cdot \mathcal{B}_t\cdot D=0$.}

Denote $u\cdot \mathcal{B}_t$ by $w=(w_{\{i,j\}})\in\mathbb{F}^{\binom{t}{2}}$, whose support is $S$.
As  $\emptyset\neq S\subseteq H$ and $H$ is acyclic, we can find $s_0\in [t]$ whose degree in $S$ is one, i.e., there exists a unique edge $\{i_0,j_0\}\in S$ such that $s_0\in \{i_0,j_0\}$. Then, the $s_0$-th entry of $w\cdot D$ is
\[
\sum_{\{i,j\}\in \binom{[t]}{2}} w_{\{i,j\}} D_{\{i,j\},s_0} = w_{\{i_0,j_0\}} D_{\{i_0,j_0\},s_0}=\pm  w_{\{i_0,j_0\}}\neq 0,
\]
which is a contradiction as $w\cdot D= u\cdot \mathcal{B}_t\cdot D=0$.
nodes.section: 3 Connection to Tree Packing and an Intermediate Result
nodes.statement_short: If direction by contradiction.

nodes.name: Contradiction hypothesis
nodes.statement:
Assume to the contrary that we can remove from  $\mathcal{B}_t$ some columns labeled by an acyclic subgraph $H$ of $K_t$ and reduce the row rank.
Let $\mathcal{B}'_t$ be the submatrix of $\mathcal{B}_t$ after the removal of the columns labeled by  $H$. The rows of   $\mathcal{B}'_t$ are linearly dependent by assumption. Hence, there exists a nonzero vector $u\in\mathbb{F}^{ inom{t-1}{2}}$ such that $u\cdot\mathcal{B}'_t=0$. As $u
eq 0$ and the rows of $\mathcal{B}_t$ are linearly independent, we have $u\cdot\mathcal{B}_t
eq 0$. Let $S\subseteq  inom{[t]}{2}$ be the support of $u\cdot\mathcal{B}_t$, where the support of a vector of length $n$ is the subset of $[n]$ that records the indices of its nonzero coordinates. As $u\cdot\mathcal{B}_t
eq 0$ and $u\cdot\mathcal{B}'_t=0$, we have $\emptyset
eq S\subseteq H$.
nodes.section: 3 Connection to Tree Packing and an Intermediate Result
nodes.statement_short: A nonzero left kernel vector of $\mathcal{B}'_t$ has support $S\subseteq H$.

nodes.name: Incidence matrix D
nodes.section: 3 Connection to Tree Packing and an Intermediate Result
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the incidence matrix $D$ and verify $\mathcal{B}_tD=0$.

nodes.name: Leaf contradiction
nodes.statement:
Denote $u\cdot \mathcal{B}_t$ by $w=(w_{\{i,j\}})\in\mathbb{F}^{\binom{t}{2}}$, whose support is $S$.
As  $\emptyset\neq S\subseteq H$ and $H$ is acyclic, we can find $s_0\in [t]$ whose degree in $S$ is one, i.e., there exists a unique edge $\{i_0,j_0\}\in S$ such that $s_0\in \{i_0,j_0\}$. Then, the $s_0$-th entry of $w\cdot D$ is
\[
\sum_{\{i,j\}\in \binom{[t]}{2}} w_{\{i,j\}} D_{\{i,j\},s_0} = w_{\{i_0,j_0\}} D_{\{i_0,j_0\},s_0}=\pm  w_{\{i_0,j_0\}}\neq 0,
\]
which is a contradiction as $w\cdot D= u\cdot \mathcal{B}_t\cdot D=0$.
nodes.section: 3 Connection to Tree Packing and an Intermediate Result
nodes.statement_short: A leaf of the acyclic support gives a nonzero entry of $wD$, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Only-if direction
nodes.statement:
Now we prove the only if direction.
It suffices to prove that removing from $\mathcal{B}_t$ a set of columns labeled by a cycle $C$ of $K_t$ will reduce its row rank by at least $1$. Let us orient the edges of $C$ to make it an oriented cycle, which by abuse of notation is also denoted by $C$.
Since the rows of $\mathcal{B}_t$ form a basis of \black{the cycle space} $C(K_t)$, there is a nonzero vector $u\in\mathbb{F}^{\binom{t-1}{2}}$ such that $u\cdot\mathcal{B}_t=u^C$. \black{Note that $u^C$ is a vector of length $\binom{t}{2}$ with support being exactly $C$, i.e., for $\{i,j\}\in\binom{[t]}{2}$, $u^C_{\{i,j\}}\neq 0$ if and only if $\{i,j\}\in C$.} Let $\mathcal{B}'_t$ be the submatrix of $\mathcal{B}_t$ after the removal of the columns labeled by $C$. Then it is not hard to check that $u\cdot\mathcal{B}'_t=0$, which implies that the rows of $\mathcal{B}'_t$ are linearly dependent, as needed.
nodes.section: 3 Connection to Tree Packing and an Intermediate Result
nodes.statement_short: Only-if direction via a cycle vector.

nodes.name: Reduction to a cycle
nodes.statement: It suffices to prove that removing from $\mathcal{B}_t$ a set of columns labeled by a cycle $C$ of $K_t$ will reduce its row rank by at least $1$.
nodes.section: 3 Connection to Tree Packing and an Intermediate Result
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to removing the columns of a cycle.

nodes.name: Orient the cycle
nodes.statement: Let us orient the edges of $C$ to make it an oriented cycle, which by abuse of notation is also denoted by $C$.
nodes.section: 3 Connection to Tree Packing and an Intermediate Result
nodes.statement_short: Orient the cycle.

nodes.name: Cycle vector in row space
nodes.statement: Since the rows of $\mathcal{B}_t$ form a basis of \black{the cycle space} $C(K_t)$, there is a nonzero vector $u\in\mathbb{F}^{\binom{t-1}{2}}$ such that $u\cdot\mathcal{B}_t=u^C$. \black{Note that $u^C$ is a vector of length $\binom{t}{2}$ with support being exactly $C$, i.e., for $\{i,j\}\in\binom{[t]}{2}$, $u^C_{\{i,j\}}\neq 0$ if and only if $\{i,j\}\in C$.}
nodes.section: 3 Connection to Tree Packing and an Intermediate Result
nodes.statement_short: The cycle vector $u^C$ is a combination of rows, supported exactly on $C$.

nodes.name: Rank drops
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{B}'_t$ be the submatrix of $\mathcal{B}_t$ after the removal of the columns labeled by $C$. Then it is not hard to check that $u\cdot\mathcal{B}'_t=0$, which implies that the rows of $\mathcal{B}'_t$ are linearly dependent, as needed.
nodes.section: 3 Connection to Tree Packing and an Intermediate Result
nodes.statement_short: The combination vanishes on the remaining columns, so rank drops.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement:
If $t=2$, then $M_{k,(I_1,I_2)}$ is a $k\times k$ Vandermonde matrix, which is nonsingular, so assume $t\ge 3$.
For the rest of the proof, we will consider the matrix $M' = M'_{k,(I_1, \ldots, I_t)}$ discussed above, and show that it is nonsingular.
nodes.section: 3 Connection to Tree Packing and an Intermediate Result
nodes.statement_short: Dispose of $t=2$; work with the permuted matrix $M'$.

nodes.name: Recall G
nodes.section: 3 Connection to Tree Packing and an Intermediate Result
nodes.statement_short: Recall $G$ and the variable set $S$.

nodes.name: Bijection phi
nodes.statement:
For $1\le i<j\le t$, fix an arbitrary one-to-one correspondence between the $|I_i \cap I_j|$ edges connecting $v_i,v_{j}$ and the $|I_i \cap I_j|$  variables $x_s \in S$ so that $s\in I_i\cap I_{j}$.
Since any three distinct subsets $I_i,I_{j},I_{\ell}$ have empty intersection, this yields a one-to-one correspondence $$\phi:E(G)\longrightarrow \{x_s:s\in S\},$$
between the $(t-1)k$ edges of $G$ and the $(t-1)k$ variables with indices in $S$.
nodes.section: 3 Connection to Tree Packing and an Intermediate Result
nodes.statement_short: Biject the edges of $G$ with the variables in $S$.

nodes.name: Tree decomposition
nodes.statement: By Claim \ref{claim-spanning-tree}, the edges of $G$ can be partitioned into $k$ edge-disjoint spanning trees $T_i$, and $G=\bigcup_{i=0}^{k-1} T_i$.
nodes.section: 3 Connection to Tree Packing and an Intermediate Result
nodes.statement_short: Partition $G$ into $k$ edge-disjoint spanning trees.

nodes.name: Plan
nodes.statement:
Observe that for each $0\le i\le k-1$, $\mathcal{C}_i$ has entries that are either zero or of the form $x_s^i$ for some $x_s \in S$.
We will show how to use the tree decomposition of $G$ to choose nonzero entries in each $\mathcal{C}_i$ so that (a) every row in the bottom part of $M'$ is chosen exactly once, and (b) when the columns chosen are removed from $M'$, the resulting submatrix of $\mathcal{B}_t$ is nonsingular.  This will mean that the product of these non-zero entries appears in the determinant expansion of $M'$.
nodes.section: 3 Connection to Tree Packing and an Intermediate Result
nodes.statement_short: Plan: choose entries of $\mathcal{C}_i$ via the trees.

nodes.name: Monomial m(x)
nodes.statement:
For each $i$, we pick $t-1$ non-zero elements from each $\mathcal{C}_i$: we choose $x_s^i$ for  $x_s \in \{\phi(e) : e \in T_i\}$.   That is, we consider all of the variables $x_s$ corresponding to edges that appear in $T_i$.
Let $m_i(x)$ denote the product of these entries:
\[ m_i(x) = \prod_{x_s \in \{\phi(e)~:~ e \in T_i\}} x_s^i. \]
Let $m(x)=\prod_{i=0}^{k-1} m_i(x)$. Since $\phi$ is a bijection, $m(x)$ is a product of $(t-1)k$ distinct entries chosen from the submatrix $\big(\mathcal{C}_i:0\le i\le k-1\big)$, and crucially, no two of them appear in the same row or column \black{--- no two in the same row because, by definition, the trees $T_i$ are pairwise edge-disjoint, and no two in the same column because a tree by definition has no parallel edges.}
nodes.section: 3 Connection to Tree Packing and an Intermediate Result
nodes.statement_short: Define the monomial $m(x)$ from the trees; entries lie in distinct rows and columns.

nodes.name: Complementary minor
nodes.statement:
To conclude the proof, it is enough to show that $m(x)$ appears as a nonvanishing term in the determinant expansion of $M'_{k,(I_1,\ldots,I_t)}$. Indeed, removing from $M'_{k,(I_1,\ldots,I_t)}$ the $(t-1)k$ rows and columns that correspond to $m(x)$, the resulting submatrix is a block diagonal matrix
\[
{\rm diag}\Big(\mathcal{B}'_t(i):~0\le i\le k-1\Big),
\]
where for each $i$, $\mathcal{B}'_t(i)$ is a square submatrix of $\mathcal{B}_t$ of order $\binom{t-1}{2}$. By construction, each $\mathcal{B}'_t(i)$ is obtained by removing from $\mathcal{B}_t$ a set of $t-1$ columns labeled by the spanning tree $T_i$.  By Claim \ref{claim-property-of-B_t}, this implies that $\mathcal{B}'_t(i)$ is nonsingular.
nodes.section: 3 Connection to Tree Packing and an Intermediate Result
nodes.statement_short: The complementary minor is block diagonal with nonsingular blocks by Claim 3.5.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of monomial
nodes.statement:
Moreover, as each of the sets $I_i \cap I_j$ are disjoint due to the assumptions of the theorem, the monomial $m(x)$ appears only once in the determinant expansion of $M'_{k,(I_1, \ldots, I_t)}$.
Consequently, the ``coefficient'' of $m(x)$ in the determinant expansion of $M'_{k,(I_1,\ldots,I_t)}$ is nonvanishing, completing the proof of the theorem.
nodes.section: 3 Connection to Tree Packing and an Intermediate Result
nodes.statement_short: Disjointness makes $m(x)$ appear once, so $\det M'\neq 0$.

nodes.name: Bad columns
nodes.statement: If an evaluation vector $\alpha\in\mathbb{F}_q^n$ is bad, then the $n\times q^k$ matrix it defines contains $t$ distinct columns defined by polynomials $f_1,\ldots,f_t$, which are  separated by at most $n-k(t-1)$ rows. Equivalently, there are at least  $k(t-1)$ rows that do not separate these $t$ columns.
nodes.statement_short: A bad vector gives $t$ columns with at least $k(t-1)$ non-separating rows.

nodes.name: Construct sets
nodes.statement_short: Assign each non-separating row to two agreeing sets; verify (a)-(c).

nodes.name: Minimal subfamily
nodes.statement:
Let \black{$s\in\{3,\ldots,t\}$} be the smallest positive integer  for which there exist a subset $S\subseteq [t]$ of size $s$ with  ${\rm wt}(I_{S})\ge k(s-1)>0$. \black{Then, by {\rm (b)} $s\ge 3$ and by {\rm (c)} $s\le t$. Therefore,} $s$ is well-defined. 
 Assume without loss of generality that $S=[s]$.
nodes.statement_short: Take the smallest violating subfamily size $s$.

nodes.name: Trim to equality
nodes.statement:
By construction and the minimality of $s$, the sets $I_1,\ldots, I_s$ satisfy properties {\rm (i)} and {\rm (ii)}. We proceed to verify that also  {\rm (iii)} holds. Note that properties {\rm (i)} and {\rm (ii)} continue to hold if one removes an element from one of the sets $I_j$, and by doing so,  the  weight ${\rm wt}(I_{[s]})$
    can reduce by at most one.   Hence, by iteratively removing elements from the sets $I_j$, one can construct sets, which we also denote by $I_1,\ldots, I_s$, that satisfy property {\rm (iii)}, while retaining properties {\rm (i)} and {\rm (ii)}.
nodes.statement_short: Minimality gives (i),(ii); remove elements to reach equality (iii).

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 3.1
nodes.statement: Since the subsets $I_1,\ldots,I_{s}\subseteq [n]$ satisfy the  three assumptions of Theorem \ref{theorem-weaker}, it holds that  $M_{k,(I_1,\ldots,I_{s})}$ is a nonsingular matrix.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 3.1 gives nonsingularity.

nodes.name: Degree bound
nodes.statement:
\black{Moreover, it follows by Claim \ref{cl:size} that $M_{k,(I_1,\ldots,I_{s})}$ is a square matrix of order $k\binom{s}{2}$. It remains to prove the claimed upper bound on the degree of the determinant. As $M_{k,(I_1,\ldots,I_{s})}$ is a square matrix of order $k\binom{s}{2}$, by Definition \ref{Def-matrix-general} the lower (variable) part ${\rm diag}\big(V_k(I_i\cap I_j): \{i,j\}\in \binom{[s]}{2}\big)$ consists of exactly $(s-1)k$ rows. According to \eqref{vandermonde}, every entry of ${\rm diag}\big(V_k(I_i\cap I_j): \{i,j\}\in \binom{[s]}{2}\big)$ is a monomial of degree at most $k-1$. Therefore, the total degree of the determinant cannot exceed $(s-1)k(k-1)<k^2s\le kt$, as needed,}

thereby completing the proof of {\rm (i)}-{\rm (iv)}.
nodes.statement_short: Square by Claim 3.3; bound the determinant degree.

nodes.name: Triangle identity
nodes.statement_short: Telescoping identity for differences.

nodes.name: Recall rows
nodes.statement: Recall that the row vectors of $\mathcal{B}_{s}$ correspond to the oriented triangles $\Delta_{ijs}$.
nodes.statement_short: Rows of $\mathcal{B}_s$ are triangles through $s$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement_short: Conclude the kernel equation.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: To prove the lemma, it suffices to show that the matrix  $M_{k,(I_1,\ldots,I_{s})}(\alpha)$ has a nontrivial kernel. Towards this end, let $f_1,\ldots,f_{s}$ be the $s$  distinct polynomials that correspond to the set $S=[s]$ found in the proof of  Lemma \ref{main-lemma}. \black{Note that the polynomials $f_1,\ldots,f_s$ correspond to subsets $I_1,\ldots,I_s$ that satisfy assumptions (i)-(iv) of Lemma \ref{main-lemma}}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to exhibiting a kernel vector; take the polynomials from Lemma 4.3.

nodes.name: Difference vector
nodes.statement:
We view a polynomial of degree at most $k-1$ also as a   vector of length $k$  defined by its $k$ coefficients, where for $1\le i\le k$, the $i$-th coordinate of the vector is the coefficient of the monomial $x^{i-1}$ in that polynomial.  
Let  $f=(f_i-f_j: 1\leq i<j\leq s)\in\mathbb{F}_q^{\binom{s}{2}k}$, as defined in the statement of Lemma \ref{lem:required}.
nodes.statement_short: Define the difference vector $f$.

nodes.name: Kernel claim
nodes.statement:
We claim that $M_{k,(I_1,\ldots,I_{s})}(\alpha)\cdot f^T=0$. First of all, it follows by Lemma \ref{lem:required} that

\begin{equation} (\mathcal{B}_s\otimes \mathcal{I}_k)\cdot f^T=0.
\end{equation}

\noindent Moreover, observe that by definition, for any $\ell\in I_i\cap I_j$ we have $f_i(\alpha_{\ell})=f_j(\alpha_{\ell})$, which implies that $0=f_i(\alpha_{\ell})-f_j(\alpha_{\ell})=(f_i-f_j)(\alpha_{\ell})=(f_i-f_j)(\alpha_{\ell})$. Therefore  $V_k(I_i\cap I_j)\cdot f_{ij}^T=0$, which implies that
\begin{equation} {\rm diag}\Big(V_k(I_i\cap I_j): \{i,j\}\in \binom{[s]}{2}\Big)\cdot f^T=0.
\end{equation}

\noindent Combining \eqref{first-half} and \eqref{second-half} we conclude that $M_{k,(I_1,\ldots,I_{s})}(\alpha)\cdot f^T=0$, completing the proof of the claim.
nodes.statement_short: Show $f$ is in the kernel.

nodes.name: Top half
nodes.statement_short: Top half vanishes by Lemma 4.4.

nodes.name: Bottom half
nodes.statement_short: Agreement on $I_i\cap I_j$ kills the Vandermonde rows.

nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement: \noindent Combining \eqref{first-half} and \eqref{second-half} we conclude that $M_{k,(I_1,\ldots,I_{s})}(\alpha)\cdot f^T=0$, completing the proof of the claim.
nodes.statement_short: Combine both halves.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: We give an upper bound on the number of bad evaluation vectors that do not define a strongly $t$-perfect hash matrix.
nodes.statement_short: Goal: bound the number of bad vectors.

nodes.name: Family M
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathcal{M}$ be the set of  $s$-wise intersection matrix $M_{k,(I_1,\ldots,I_{s})}$ that satisfy conditions {\rm (i)}-{\rm (iv)} of Lemma \ref{main-lemma} for any $s\in \{3,\ldots, t\}$.
It is clear that any  $s$-wise intersection matrix $M_{k,(I_1,\ldots,I_s)}$ is completely determined by the subsets $I_1,\ldots,I_s$, therefore the size of $\mathcal{M}$    is at most  $2^{nt}$.
nodes.statement_short: The family $\mathcal{M}$ of candidate matrices has size at most $2^{nt}$.

nodes.name: Zero-set bound
nodes.statement:
By Lemma \ref{main-lemma}, for any bad evaluation vector $\alpha\in\mathbb{F}_q^n$ there exists a matrix $M\in\mathcal{M}$ whose determinant is a nonzero polynomial in $\mathbb{F}_q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ of degree less than $k^2t$, \black{and moreover},  by Lemma \ref{main-lemma-2}, it holds that $\det(M)(\alpha)=0$. Therefore, the set of bad evaluation vectors is contained in the union of the zero sets of the polynomials $\det(M),~M\in\mathcal{M}$, which by Lemma \ref{zeros}, is of size at most
$$|\mathcal{M}|\cdot(k^2t)q^{n-1}\le (2^{nt}k^2t)q^{n-1}=O_{n,t}(q^{n-1}).$$
nodes.statement_short: Bad vectors are zeros of some $\det M$; Schwartz-Zippel bounds their number.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: The result follows by observing that the number of evaluation vectors, i.e., the number of  vectors in $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ with pairwise distinct coordinates is  $\frac{q!}{(q-n)!}=\Theta_n(q^n)$. Hence, for sufficiently large $q$ there exist many evaluation vectors that are not bad, and the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Compare with $\Theta_n(q^n)$ evaluation vectors.

nodes.name: RS matrices are linear
nodes.statement: It is clear that any $n\times q^k$ matrix $M$ given by an $[n,k]$-RS code is linear, as we may write $M=V_k(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)\cdot Q$, where $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)$ is the evaluation vector,  $V_k(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)$ is the associated $n\times k$ Vandermonde matrix as defined in \eqref{vandermonde}, and $Q$ is the $k\times q^k$ matrix whose columns are formed by the $q^k$ distinct vectors of $\mathbb{F}_q^k$.
nodes.statement_short: RS matrices are linear.

nodes.name: Blackburn's bound
nodes.statement: The statement on the optimality follows  from  Theorem 4 of \cite{Blackburn1998Optimal} which claims that  any linear $N\times q^k$ matrix that has the property that any set of $t$ columns is separated by at least one row, satisfies $N\ge k(t-1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Invoke Blackburn's bound $N\ge k(t-1)$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: By this result, the restriction to the first   $k(t-1)-1$ rows of an $n\times q^k$ linear matrix, contains a set of $t$ columns that are not separated at all. Hence, this set of columns is separated by at most $n-k(t-1)+1$ rows of the $n\times q^k$ linear matrix, and the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: The first $k(t-1)-1$ rows leave some $t$ columns unseparated.

nodes.name: Choices of J
nodes.statement: There are at most $2^t$ choices of $J$.
nodes.statement_short: At most $2^t$ choices of $J$.

nodes.name: Define T_j
nodes.statement:
Now fix $J\subseteq [t]$.
For $j\in [n]$, let $T_j=\{i\in J: j\in I'_i\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $J$ and define $T_j$.

nodes.name: Choices of T_j
nodes.statement:
Note that we have $|T_j|\leq 2$ for all $j\in [n]$ by Condition~(1) of Lemma~\ref{lem_subset}.
So for each $j\in [n]$, the number of choices of $T_j$ is at most $1+t+\binom{t}{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Each $T_j$ has at most $1+t+\binom{t}{2}$ choices.

nodes.name: T_j determine I_i'
nodes.statement: Also note that the sets $I_i'$ are determined by the sets $T_j$ by $I_i'=\{j\in [n]: i\in T_j\}$.
nodes.statement_short: The $T_j$ determine the $I_i'$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: So the number of choices of $(J, (I_i')_{i\in J})$ is at most $2^t(1+t+\binom{t}{2})^n$.
nodes.statement_short: Multiply the counts.

nodes.name: Outline
nodes.statement: At the high level, the proof works as follows: First, we show that with high probability, a certain square matrix $M_{k, (I_i')_{i\in J}}(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)$ has full rank. Next, we show that whenever the matrix has full rank,  $\mathsf{RS}_{n,k,q}(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)$ is list-recoverable up to relative distance $1-\varepsilon$ as claimed by Theorem~\ref{list-recover-main}. More precisely, we prove the contrapositive, i.e., if $\mathsf{RS}_{n,k,q}(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)$ is not list-recoverable up to relative distance $1-\varepsilon$, then there exists a nonzero vector $f$ in the kernel of $M_{k, (I_i')_{i\in J}}(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)$. The proof that such a vector $f$ exists uses Lemma~\ref{lem_subset}, Lemma \ref{lem:required}, and the same ideas in the proof of Lemma~\ref{main-lemma-2}.
nodes.statement_short: Outline: full rank w.h.p., and full rank implies list-recoverability.

nodes.name: Two conditions
nodes.statement:
Let $t=L+1$. Consider the following two conditions:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item $\alpha_i\neq \alpha_j$ for all distinct $i,j\in [n]$.
\item For all $J\subseteq [t]$ and $(I_i')_{i\in J}$ satisfying Conditions~(1)--(3) of Lemma~\ref{lem_subset}, we have
\[
\det(M_{k, (I_i')_{i\in J}}(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n))\neq 0,
\] where $M_{k, (I_i')_{i\in J}}$ denotes the  $\binom{|J|}{2}k\times \binom{|J|}{2}k$ variable matrix\footnote{The number of rows of $M_{k, (I_i')_{i\in J}}$ is $\binom{|J|-1}{2}k + \sum_{\{i,j\}\in \binom{J}{2}} |I'_i\cap I'_j|$, which equals $\binom{|J|-1}{2}k+\sum_{i\in J} |I'_i|-|\bigcup_{i\in J} I'_i|=\binom{|J|-1}{2}k+{\rm wt}(I'_J)$ by Condition~(1) of Lemma~\ref{lem_subset}. This number further equals $\binom{|J|-1}{2}k+(|J|-1)k=\binom{|J|}{2}k$ by Condition~(3) of Lemma~\ref{lem_subset}.}
\[
M_{k, (I_i')_{i\in J}}=\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    \mathcal{B}_{|J|}\otimes \mathcal{I}_k  \\\hline
  {\rm diag}\Big(V_k(I_i'\cap I_j'): \{i,j\}\in \binom{J}{2}\Big) \\
  \end{array}
\right).
\]
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the two good-event conditions.

nodes.name: Condition 1
nodes.statement:
$\alpha_i\neq \alpha_j$ for all distinct $i,j\in [n]$.
\item
nodes.statement_short: Distinct evaluation points.

nodes.name: Condition 2
nodes.statement:
For all $J\subseteq [t]$ and $(I_i')_{i\in J}$ satisfying Conditions~(1)--(3) of Lemma~\ref{lem_subset}, we have
\[
\det(M_{k, (I_i')_{i\in J}}(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n))\neq 0,
\] where $M_{k, (I_i')_{i\in J}}$ denotes the  $\binom{|J|}{2}k\times \binom{|J|}{2}k$ variable matrix\footnote{The number of rows of $M_{k, (I_i')_{i\in J}}$ is $\binom{|J|-1}{2}k + \sum_{\{i,j\}\in \binom{J}{2}} |I'_i\cap I'_j|$, which equals $\binom{|J|-1}{2}k+\sum_{i\in J} |I'_i|-|\bigcup_{i\in J} I'_i|=\binom{|J|-1}{2}k+{\rm wt}(I'_J)$ by Condition~(1) of Lemma~\ref{lem_subset}. This number further equals $\binom{|J|-1}{2}k+(|J|-1)k=\binom{|J|}{2}k$ by Condition~(3) of Lemma~\ref{lem_subset}.}
\[
M_{k, (I_i')_{i\in J}}=\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    \mathcal{B}_{|J|}\otimes \mathcal{I}_k  \\\hline
  {\rm diag}\Big(V_k(I_i'\cap I_j'): \{i,j\}\in \binom{J}{2}\Big) \\
  \end{array}
\right).
\]
nodes.statement_short: All relevant determinants are nonzero at $\alpha$.

nodes.name: Condition 1 probability
nodes.statement: The first condition is satisfied with probability at least $1-\binom{n}{2}/q$.
nodes.statement_short: Condition 1 holds w.p. $1-\binom{n}{2}/q$.

nodes.name: Condition 2 probability
nodes.statement:
For the second condition, consider fixed $J\subseteq [t]$ and $(I_i')_{i\in J}$  satisfying Conditions~(1)--(3) of Lemma~\ref{lem_subset}.
We  know $\det(M_{k, (I_i')_{i\in J}})\neq 0$ by Theorem~\ref{theorem-weaker}.
 Also note that $\det(M_{k, (I_i')_{i\in J}})$ is a multivariate polynomial of total degree at most $(|J|-1)k(k-1)\leq Lk^2$.
So by Lemma \ref{zeros}, $\det(M_{k, (I_i')_{i\in J}})(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)\neq 0$ holds with probability at least
$1-Lk^2/q$ for  fixed $J$ and $(I_i')_{i\in J}$. The number of choices of $(J, (I_i')_{i\in J})$ is at most  $2^t(1+t+\binom{t}{2})^n$ by Lemma~\ref{lem_counting}. By the union bound, the two conditions are simultaneously satisfied with probability at least
\[
1-\binom{n}{2}/q-2^t\left(1+t+\binom{t}{2}\right)^n Lk^2/q=1-o(1)
\]
over the random choices of $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$, where we use the assumption that $q\geq 2^{c'(L+n\log L)}$ and $c'>0$ is a large enough constant.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 3.1, Schwartz-Zippel and Lemma 5.5 with a union bound.

nodes.name: Fix good alpha
nodes.statement:
Fix $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\in{\mathbb{F}}_q$ that satisfy the above two conditions.
By the first condition, the code $\mathsf{RS}_{n,k,q}(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)$ has rate exactly $k/n$.
It remains to show that $\mathsf{RS}_{n,k,q}(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)$ is  list-recoverable up to relative distance $1-\varepsilon$ with input list size $\ell$ and output list size $L$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix good $\alpha$; rate is $k/n$.

nodes.name: Contradiction hypothesis
nodes.statement:
Assume to the contrary that this does not hold. Then there exist $t$ distinct polynomials $f_1,\dots,f_t\in {\mathbb{F}}_q[x]$ of degree less than $k$ and sets $S_1,\dots,S_n$ of size $\ell$ such that for all $i\in [t]$, the cardinality of the set
\[
I_i:=\{j\in [n]:  f_i(\alpha_j)\in S_j\}
\]
is at least $\varepsilon n$.
nodes.statement_short: A failure gives $t$ polynomials with large agreement sets $I_i$.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 5.3
nodes.statement:
As $t=L+1\geq (1+\delta) \ell/\varepsilon$ and
$k/n\leq \frac{\varepsilon}{c \sqrt{\ell}( \frac{1+\delta}{\delta } )(\log(\frac{1}{\varepsilon})+\log( \frac{1+\delta}{\delta })+1)}$,
we have
\[
\mathrm{wt}_\ell(I_{[t]})\stackrel{\eqref{eq_weightell}}{\geq } t \varepsilon n-\ell n \geq \frac{\delta}{1+\delta} \cdot t\varepsilon n\geq  \left(c\sqrt{\ell}\left(\log\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right)+\log\left( \frac{1+\delta}{\delta }\right)+1\right)\right)\cdot tk.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem_subset},  there exist $J\subseteq [t]$ and   $(I_i')_{i\in J}$
such that $|J|\geq 2$, $I_i'\subseteq I_i$ for $i\in J$,  and Conditions~(1)--(4) of Lemma~\ref{lem_subset} are satisfied, where we let $c_{i,j}=f_i(\alpha_j)\in S_j$ for $i\in [t]$ and $j\in I_t$.
nodes.statement_short: The generalized weight is large, so Lemma 5.3 applies.

nodes.name: Difference vector
nodes.statement: Let $f=(f_i-f_j: \{i,j\}\in \binom{J}{2}, i<j)\in {\mathbb{F}}_q^{\binom{|J|}{2}k}$, as defined in the statement of Lemma \ref{lem:required}. As $|J|\geq 2$ and $f_1,\dots, f_t$ are distinct, we have $f\neq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the nonzero difference vector $f$.

nodes.name: Kernel claim
nodes.statement:
We claim that
\begin{equation} M_{k, (I_i')_{i\in J}}(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n) \cdot f^T=0.
\end{equation}
To see this, first note that it follows by Lemma \ref{lem:required} that $(\mathcal{B}_{|J|}\otimes \mathcal{I}_k)\cdot f^T=0$.

Now consider a row $v$ of the submatrix
\[
{\rm diag}\Big(V_k(I_i'\cap I_j'): \{i,j\}\in \binom{J}{2}\Big)(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n),
\]
 of $M_{k, (I_i')_{i\in J}}(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)$, which corresponds to some $\{i,j\}\in \binom{J}{2}$ with $i<j$ and $s\in I_i'\cap I_j'$. By definition, we have $v \cdot f^T=(f_i-f_j)(\alpha_s)=f_i(\alpha_s)-f_j(\alpha_s)$, i.e., the row $v$ represents the linear constraint $f_i(\alpha_s)-f_j(\alpha_s)=0$.
By Condition~(4) of Lemma~\ref{lem_subset}, we have $f_i(\alpha_s)=c_{i,s}=c_{j,s}=f_j(\alpha_s)$.
So $v\cdot f^T=f_i(\alpha_s)-f_j(\alpha_s)=0$.
This proves \eqref{eq_lineqns}.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: $f$ is in the kernel.

nodes.name: Top half
nodes.statement: To see this, first note that it follows by Lemma \ref{lem:required} that $(\mathcal{B}_{|J|}\otimes \mathcal{I}_k)\cdot f^T=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Top half vanishes by Lemma 4.4.

nodes.name: Bottom row
nodes.statement:
Now consider a row $v$ of the submatrix
\[
{\rm diag}\Big(V_k(I_i'\cap I_j'): \{i,j\}\in \binom{J}{2}\Big)(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n),
\]
 of $M_{k, (I_i')_{i\in J}}(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)$, which corresponds to some $\{i,j\}\in \binom{J}{2}$ with $i<j$ and $s\in I_i'\cap I_j'$. By definition, we have $v \cdot f^T=(f_i-f_j)(\alpha_s)=f_i(\alpha_s)-f_j(\alpha_s)$, i.e., the row $v$ represents the linear constraint $f_i(\alpha_s)-f_j(\alpha_s)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: A bottom row encodes $f_i(\alpha_s)=f_j(\alpha_s)$.

nodes.name: Bottom row vanishes
nodes.statement:
By Condition~(4) of Lemma~\ref{lem_subset}, we have $f_i(\alpha_s)=c_{i,s}=c_{j,s}=f_j(\alpha_s)$.
So $v\cdot f^T=f_i(\alpha_s)-f_j(\alpha_s)=0$.
This proves \eqref{eq_lineqns}.
nodes.statement_short: Condition (4) makes each bottom row vanish.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: Finally, by \eqref{eq_lineqns}, we have $\det(M_{k, (I_i')_{i\in J}}(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n))=0$. But this contradicts the choice of $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$.
nodes.statement_short: The determinant vanishes, contradicting the choice of $\alpha$.

nodes.name: Recall hypotheses
nodes.statement:
Let $k,n,t,\ell\in{\mathbb{N}}^+$, $\varepsilon\in (0,1]$, $\delta>0$, $I_1,\dots,I_t$,
$S_1,\dots, S_n$,
and $c_{i,j}$ for $i\in [t]$ and $j\in I_i$
be as in Lemma~\ref{lem_subset}.
In particular, we have $t\geq (1+\delta)\ell/\varepsilon$,
 $|I_i|\geq \varepsilon n$ for $i\in [t]$, and
\begin{equation} \mathrm{wt}_\ell(I_{[t]})\geq \left(c\sqrt{\ell}\left(\log\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right)+\log\left( \frac{1+\delta}{\delta }\right)+1\right)\right)\cdot tk.
\end{equation}
where $c>0$ is a large enough absolute constant.
We will choose $J\subseteq [t]$ to be a random set and  carefully construct the sets $I'_i$, $i\in J$, such that the conditions in Lemma~\ref{lem_subset} are satisfied.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the hypotheses of Lemma 5.3.

nodes.name: Define U_j
nodes.statement_short: Define multiplicity sets $U_j$.

nodes.name: Uniform case
nodes.statement:
Assume for a moment that there exists an integer $K\in{\mathbb{N}}^+$ such that $\max\{|U_j|-\ell, 0\}$ equals either $K$ or zero for all $j\in [n]$. Then by \eqref{eq_weight_ell}, the number of $j\in [n]$ for which $\max\{|U_j|-\ell, 0\}=K$ holds (or equivalently, $|U_j|=K+\ell$ holds) is precisely $\mathrm{wt}(I_{[t]})/K$.
The next lemma extends this fact to the general case with only logarithmic loss.
nodes.statement_short: Uniform-excess heuristic motivating Lemma 5.6.

nodes.name: Weight lower bound
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound the generalized weight.

nodes.name: Buckets
nodes.statement:
For $i=0,1,2,\dots$, let $B_i=\{j\in [n]: 2^i\leq |U_j|-\ell <2^{i+1}\}$.
Then
\[
\mathrm{wt}_\ell(I_{[t]})=\sum_{j=1}^n \max\{|U_j|-\ell, 0\}=\sum_{i=0}^{\lceil\log t\rceil-1} \sum_{j\in B_i}  (|U_j|-\ell).
\]
nodes.statement_short: Dyadic buckets $B_i$.

nodes.name: Discard light buckets
nodes.statement:
Let $d=\lfloor \log ( \frac{\delta}{1+\delta} \cdot t\varepsilon/2) \rfloor$. Note that $d$ could be negative (possibly $\frac{\delta}{1+\delta} \cdot t\varepsilon/2\in(0,1)$).
Then
\[
\sum_{0\leq i<d} \sum_{j\in B_i}  (|U_j|-\ell)\leq n 2^d \leq  \frac{\delta}{1+\delta} \cdot t\varepsilon n/2  \stackrel{\eqref{eq_weight_lb}}{\leq} \mathrm{wt}_\ell(I_{[t]})/2.
\]
Therefore
\begin{equation} \sum_{i=\max\{d,0\}}^{\lceil\log t\rceil-1} \sum_{j\in B_i} (|U_j|-\ell) \geq \mathrm{wt}_\ell(I_{[t]})/2.
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Light buckets contribute at most half.

nodes.name: Heavy bucket
nodes.statement:
Let $\Delta=\lceil\log t\rceil-\max\{d,0\}= O(\log(\frac{1}{\varepsilon})+\log( \frac{1+\delta}{\delta })+1)$.
By \eqref{eq_truncate}, there exists an integer $i_0$ such that $\max\{d,0\}\leq i_0\leq \lceil\log t\rceil-1$ and
\begin{equation} \sum_{j\in B_{i_0}}  (|U_j|-\ell)\geq \frac{\mathrm{wt}_\ell(I_{[t]})}{2\Delta}.
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Pigeonhole a heavy bucket among $\Delta$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement:
Choose $K=2^{i_0}$. Then $K\leq |U_j|-\ell<2K$ for all $j\in B_{i_0}$.
The upper bound $  |U_j|-\ell <2K$  for  $j\in B_{i_0}$, together with \eqref{eq_i0},    implies $|B_{i_0}|\geq  \frac{\mathrm{wt}_\ell(I_{[t]})}{4K \Delta}$.
So the number of $j\in [n]$ satisfying  $|U_j|\geq K+\ell$ is at least $\frac{\mathrm{wt}_\ell(I_{[t]})}{4K\Delta}=\Omega\left(\frac{\mathrm{wt}_\ell(I_{[t]})}{K(\log(\frac{1}{\varepsilon})+\log( \frac{1+\delta}{\delta })+1)}\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Set $K=2^{i_0}$ and count coordinates.

nodes.name: Derivative
nodes.statement_short: Bound the derivative of $f$.

nodes.name: Integrate
nodes.statement_short: Integrate the derivative bound.

nodes.name: Case small x
nodes.statement:
If $x\le \frac{1}{p}$, we have $(1-p)^x\ge (1-p)^{1/p}\ge 1/4$, as $(1-p)^{1/p}$ is decreasing with $p$, and thus is minimized at $p=\frac{1}{2}$.
    Hence, we have $f(x)\le 1-\frac{1}{8}p^2x^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Case $x\le 1/p$.

nodes.name: Case large x
nodes.statement: By \eqref{eq:calc}, $f(y)$ is decreasing and thus maximized at $y=1/p$ on the interval $[1/p,\infty)$, so for $x\ge 1/p$, we have $f(x)\le f(1/p) =(1-p)^{1/p}(1+1) \le \frac{2}{e}$.
nodes.statement_short: Case $x\ge 1/p$ by monotonicity.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement:
Fix $j\in A$.
  It suffices to prove that $\Pr[j\in A_J]\ge c$ for some constant $c$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a constant lower bound on $\Pr[j\in A_J]$.

nodes.name: Color classes
nodes.statement:
Suppose $S_j=\{c_1,\dots,c_\ell\}$. For $r=1,\dots,\ell$, let
  \[
   U_j^{(r)}:=\{i\in U_j: c_{i,j}=c_r\}
   \quad\text{and}\quad t_r\coloneqq \max\{|U_j\ind{r}|-1,0\}.
   \]
   Then $U_j=\bigcup_{r=1}^\ell U_j^{(r)}$.
   Let $K'\coloneqq \sum_{r=1}^{\ell} t_j$.
   Since $j\in A$ and $U_j=\bigcup_{r=1}^\ell U_j^{(r)}$, we have
   \[
   K'=\sum_{r=1}^{\ell} t_j \ge |U_j|-\ell \ge K.
   \]
nodes.statement_short: Split $U_j$ into color classes; define $t_r$ and $K'\ge K$.

nodes.name: Per-class probability
nodes.statement_short: Probability that a color class gets at most one sample.

nodes.name: Product formula
nodes.statement:
By definition, $U_j\ind{1},\dots,U_j\ind{\ell}$ are disjoint. So the events that $|U_j\ind{r}\cap J|\ge 2$ are independent.
   Thus, the probability that $j\in A_J$ is
   \begin{align}
    \Pr[j\in A_J]
    =\Pr\left[\bigvee_{r=1}^\ell |U_j\ind{r}\cap J|\geq 2\right]
    = 1 - \prod_{r=1}^{\ell} \Pr[|U_j\ind{r}\cap J|\le 1]
    &= 1 - \prod_{r=1}^{\ell} (1-p)^{t_r}(1+t_rp)\\
    &= 1 - (1-p)^{K'}\prod_{r=1}^{\ell} (1+t_rp).
   \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Independence across classes gives a product formula.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: We now bound this below by a constant.
nodes.statement_short: Goal: constant lower bound.

nodes.name: Case K' <= l
nodes.statement_short: Case $K'\le\ell$: smoothing argument.

nodes.name: Case K' > l
nodes.statement:
Now suppose $K' > \ell$.
   Note that $p = \min\{\sqrt{\ell}/(2K),\frac{1}{2}\} \ge \sqrt{\ell}/(2K')$.
   As $\log (1+xp)$ is concave for nonnegative real numbers $x$, we have that $f(x_1,\dots,x_\ell)=\prod_{r=1}^{\ell} (1+x_rp)$ subject to $x_1+\cdots+x_\ell=K'$ is maximized when all the $x_i$'s are equal.
   Hence,
   \begin{align}
    \Pr[j\in A_J]
    = 1 - (1-p)^{K'}\prod_{r=1}^{\ell} (1+t_rp)
    &\ge 1 - (1-p)^{K'}\left( 1 + \frac{K'}{\ell}p \right)^{\ell}  \nonumber\\
    &= 1 - \left(\left((1-p)^{K'/\ell}\right)\left( 1 + \frac{K'}{\ell}p \right)\right)^{\ell}
   \end{align}
   as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Case $K'>\ell$: concavity equalizes the $t_r$.

nodes.name: Subcase small x
nodes.statement_short: Subcase $x\le 1/p$ via Lemma 5.7.

nodes.name: Subcase large x
nodes.statement: If $x\ge 1/p$, then by Lemma~\ref{lem:calc}, we have $\Pr[j\in A_J] \ge 1-(2/e)^\ell \ge 1-2/e$.
nodes.statement_short: Subcase $x\ge 1/p$ via Lemma 5.7.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: In all cases,  $\Pr[j\in A_J]$ is bounded below by a constant, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Constant lower bound in all cases.

nodes.name: Large A_J
nodes.statement:
Choose a random set $J\subseteq [t]$ as in  Lemma~\ref{lem_sampling}. Then ${\rm{E}}[|A_J|]=\Omega(|A|)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem_sampling}.
As $|A_J|\leq |A|$, we have $\Pr[|A_J|\geq d_2|A|]\geq d_3$ for some absolute constants $d_2,d_3>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Expectation bound gives $|A_J|\ge d_2|A|$ with constant probability.

nodes.name: Small J
nodes.statement: Observe that by Lemma~\ref{lem_sampling} and the linearity of expectation we have ${\rm{E}}[|J|]=pt=O(\sqrt{\ell}t/K)$. Moreover, by Markov's inequality we have $\Pr[|J|>d_1 \sqrt{\ell}t/K]\leq d_3/2$ for some sufficiently large constant $d_1>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Markov's inequality bounds $|J|$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: By the union bound, we know the conditions $|J|\leq d_1 \sqrt{\ell}t/K$ and $|A_J|\geq d_2|A|$ are simultaneously satisfied with probability at least $d_3/2>0$, so there exists $J\subseteq [t]$ that satisfies these two conditions.
nodes.statement_short: Union bound gives a good $J$.

nodes.name: Bound A_J
nodes.statement:
Fix $J\subseteq [t]$ as in Corollary~\ref{cor_existJ}, so that $|J|\leq d_1\sqrt{\ell}t/K$ and $|A_J|\geq d_2 |A|$.
As the constant $c$ in \eqref{eq_weightbound} is large enough, we may assume $c\geq d_0 d_1/d_2$, where $d_0$ is as in \eqref{eq_boundA}.
Then we have
\begin{equation} |A_J|\geq d_2|A|\stackrel{\eqref{eq_boundA}}{\geq} d_2  \cdot \frac{\mathrm{wt}_\ell(I_{[t]})}{d_0 K (\log(\frac{1}{\varepsilon})+\log( \frac{1+\delta}{\delta })+1)}  \stackrel{\eqref{eq_weightbound}}{\geq} (d_1\sqrt{\ell}t/K)k > (|J|-1)k.
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Combine Corollary 5.9 with (17) and (12) to get $|A_J|>(|J|-1)k$.

nodes.name: Choose pairs
nodes.statement:
For each $j\in A_J$, choose $c_j\in S_j$ and $T_j\subseteq J$ such that $|T_j|=2$ and $c_{i,j}=c_j$ for $i\in T_j$. This is possible by the definition of $A_J$ in Lemma~\ref{lem_sampling}. For $j\in [n]\setminus A_J$, let $T_j=\emptyset$.  So for $j\in [n]$, we have
\[
|T_j|=\begin{cases} 2 & j\in A_J,\\
0 & j\not\in A_J.
\end{cases}
\]
nodes.statement_short: Pick an agreeing pair $T_j$ for each $j\in A_J$.

nodes.name: Define I_i'
nodes.statement:
Let $I_i'=\{j\in [n]: i\in T_j\}\subseteq I_i$ for $i\in J$. We have
\[
\mathrm{wt}(I_J')=\sum_{j=1}^n \max\{|T_j|-1, 0\}=|A_J|\stackrel{\eqref{eq_AJ_bound}}{\geq} (|J|-1)k.
\]
Moreover, the fact $|T_j|\leq 2$ for $j\in [n]$ implies that $I'_{i}\cap I'_{i'}\cap I'_{i''}=\emptyset$ for distinct  $i,i',i''\in J$, by noting that $T_j=\{i\in J: j\in I'_i\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $I_i'$; weight equals $|A_J|$; no triple intersections.

nodes.name: Colors agree
nodes.statement: For $i\in [t]$ and $j\in I'_i$, we have $c_{i,j}=c_j$ by the definition of $I'_i$. In particular, $c_{i,j}=c_{i',j}$ for $i,i'\in [t]$ and $j\in I'_i\cap I'_{i'}$.
nodes.statement_short: Colors agree on pairwise intersections.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Finally, we have $|J|\geq 2$ as $|A_J|\geq d_2 |A|>0$. To summarize, we have proved the following weaker version of Lemma~\ref{lem_subset}.
nodes.statement_short: $|J|\ge 2$; summarize as Lemma 5.10.

nodes.name: Minimal J
nodes.statement: Choose the sets $J$ and $(I_i')_{i\in J}$ satisfying Lemma~\ref{lem_weak_subset} such that $|J|\geq 2$ is minimized.
nodes.statement_short: Take $J$ of minimal size from Lemma 5.10.

nodes.name: Trim weight
nodes.statement:
Note that removing one element from $I'_i$ for some $i\in J$ preserves (1) and (3) of Lemma~\ref{lem_weak_subset} and reduces $\mathrm{wt}(I'_J)$ by at most one.
Removing elements from the sets in $(I_i')_{i\in J}$ one by one until $\mathrm{wt}(I'_J)=(|J|-1)k$ holds. Then $J$ and $(I_i')_{i\in J}$ satisfy (1), (3), and (4) of Lemma~\ref{lem_subset}.
nodes.statement_short: Delete elements until the weight equals $(|J|-1)k$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: The minimality of $|J|$ guarantees that $\mathrm{wt}(I'_{J'})\leq (|J'|-1)k$ for all nonempty $J'\subseteq J$. (When $|J'|=1$, this holds since $\mathrm{wt}(I'_{J'})=0$.) So  $J$ and $(I_i')_{i\in J}$  satisfy (2) of Lemma~\ref{lem_subset} as well.
nodes.statement_short: Minimality gives condition (2).

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: According to \eqref{eq:weak-part} it suffices to show that for any partition $\mathcal{P}$ of the vertices of $H$, $\sum_{e\in E(H)}(\mathcal{P}(e)-1)\ge k(|\mathcal{P}|-1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the defining inequality.

nodes.name: Decompose edges
nodes.statement_short: Decompose $|e|$ along the partition.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement_short: Sum over edges and apply both hypotheses.

nodes.name: Hypergraph H
nodes.statement:
Assume Conjecture~\ref{conj:weak} is true.
Let $I_1,\dots,I_t\subseteq[n]$ be subsets satisfying the conditions of Conjecture~\ref{conjecture}.
For all $i\in [n]$, let $e_i=\{j\in [t]: i\in I_j\}$.
Let $H$ be a (multi)hypergraph with vertex set $[t]$ and edge set $E(H)=\{e_i:i\in[n]\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Build the hypergraph $H$ of coordinate memberships.

nodes.name: Claim 6.6 block
nodes.statement_short: Claim 6.6 and its proof.

nodes.name: Claim 6.7 block
nodes.statement_short: Claim 6.7 and its proof.

nodes.name: Apply conjecture
nodes.statement: By our assumption that Conjecture~\ref{conj:weak} is true, there exists a tree-assignment $G$ of $H$ that is $k$-distinguishable. Note that by definition $G$ has $k(t-1)$ edges, which are labeled by the hyperedges of $H$. Let $S\subseteq [n]$ be the subset so that $\{e_s:s\in S\}$ forms the set of those labels. Then, an edge $\{j,j'\}$ of $G$ has label $e_s$ for some $s\in S$ if and only if $s\in I_j\cap I_{j'}$.
nodes.statement_short: Conjecture 6.1 gives a $k$-distinguishable tree-assignment $G$.

nodes.name: Recall M
nodes.statement_short: Recall the intersection matrix and its column labels.

nodes.name: Permuted matrix
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the permuted matrix $M'$.

nodes.name: Fact 6.8 block
nodes.statement_short: Fact 6.8 on row structure.

nodes.name: Square submatrix
nodes.statement:
Let us consider $\binom{t}{2}k\times \binom{t}{2}k$ submatrix $M'$ of $M'_{k,(I_1,\dots,I_t)}$ obtained as follows:

\begin{enumerate}
\item Keep the top $\binom{t-1}{2}k\times \binom{t}{2}k$ submatrix $\mathcal{I}_k\otimes B_t$.
\item For every edge $\{j,j'\}$ in $G$ of label $e_s$, keep the row in $\big(\mathcal{C}_i:0\le i\le k-1\big)$ with nonzero entries $x_s^0,\dots,x_s^{k-1}$ in $\{j,j'\}$-labeled columns (this is well-defined according to Fact~\ref{fact:M'-1}).
\item Remove all other rows.
nodes.statement_short: Select a square submatrix $M'$ using the edges of $G$.

nodes.name: Keep top
nodes.statement:
Keep the top $\binom{t-1}{2}k\times \binom{t}{2}k$ submatrix $\mathcal{I}_k\otimes B_t$.
\item
nodes.statement_short: Keep the top block.

nodes.name: Keep edge rows
nodes.statement:
For every edge $\{j,j'\}$ in $G$ of label $e_s$, keep the row in $\big(\mathcal{C}_i:0\le i\le k-1\big)$ with nonzero entries $x_s^0,\dots,x_s^{k-1}$ in $\{j,j'\}$-labeled columns (this is well-defined according to Fact~\ref{fact:M'-1}).
\item
nodes.statement_short: Keep one row per edge of $G$.

nodes.name: Remove rows
nodes.statement: Remove all other rows.
nodes.statement_short: Remove the rest.

nodes.name: Square
nodes.statement: \noindent As $G$ has $k(t-1)$ edges, precisely $k(t-1)$ rows are kept in step $2$. Therefore, $M'$ has $\binom{t-1}{2}k + k(t-1) = \binom{t}{2}k$ rows and is thus square.
nodes.statement_short: The submatrix is square.

nodes.name: Plan
nodes.statement: Below we show that $M'$ has a nonzero determinant, thereby implying that $M'_{k,(I_1,\ldots,I_t)}$ and hence $M_{k,(I_1,\ldots,I_t)}$ are nonsingular, which is the claim of Conjecture~\ref{conjecture}, and thus establishing Theorem~\ref{thm:complete-2}. For that purpose, it is enough to show that there is a monomial that appears as a nonvanishing term in the determinant expansion of $M'$. To find such a monomial, we use the fact that $G$ is $k$-distinguishable.
nodes.statement_short: Plan: find a nonvanishing monomial using distinguishability.

nodes.name: Monomials
nodes.statement_short: Define monomials $x^T$ and $x^{(T_0,\dots,T_{k-1})}$.

nodes.name: Monomial equals signature
nodes.statement_short: The monomial's exponent is the signature.

nodes.name: Unique monomial
nodes.statement:
Since $G$ is $k$-distinguishable, there exists a tree decomposition $T_0,\dots,T_{k-1}$ such that for any other tree-assignment $T_0',\dots,T_{k-1}'$, we have that the signatures $v^{(T_0,\dots,T_{k-1})}\neq v^{(T_0',\dots,T_{k-1}')}$.
Thus, it follows by \eqref{equ:new-1} that the monomials $x^{(T_0,\dots,T_{k-1})}\neq x^{(T_0',\dots,T_{k-1}')}$.
nodes.statement_short: Distinguishability makes the monomial unique among decompositions.

nodes.name: Claim 6.9 statement
nodes.statement:
\begin{claim} Let $T_0,\ldots,T_{k-1}$ be spanning trees as defined above. Then, $x^{(T_0,\dots,T_{k-1})}$ appears as a nonvanishing term in the determinant expansion of $M'$.
\end{claim}
nodes.statement_short: State Claim 6.9.

nodes.name: Index entries
nodes.statement:
Proving Claim~\ref{clm:new-1} establishes the nonsingularity of $M'$ and thus, as discussed above, Theorem~\ref{thm:complete-2}. For that purpose, we identify the nonzero entries in the bottom $(t-1)k$ rows of $M'$ by tuples $(s,\{j,j'\},i)$, where $s\in S\cap (I_j\cap I_{j'})$, $\{j,j'\}\in\binom{[t]}{2}$, and $0\le i\le k-1$. Indeed, such a tuple corresponds to the entry $x_s^i$ in the $\{j,j'\}$-labeled column of $\mathcal{C}_i$.
It is worth mentioning that we used two types of labeling here: first, each column of $\mathcal{I}_k\otimes \mathcal{B}_t$ and $(\mathcal{C}_i:~0\le i\le k-1)$ is labeled by some edge $\{j,j'\}\in\binom{[t]}{2}$; second, each edge of $G$ is labeled by some variable $x_s,~s\in S$.
nodes.statement_short: Index bottom nonzero entries by tuples $(s,\{j,j'\},i)$.

nodes.name: Partial transversals
nodes.statement_short: Partial transversals and the determinant expansion.

nodes.name: Subgraphs Q_i
nodes.statement: For a partial transversal $Q$ and $0\le i\le k-1$, let $Q_i$ be the subgraph of $G$ that corresponds to the tuples $(s,\{j,j'\},i)\in Q$, namely, $$Q_i=\left\{\{j,j'\}\in \binom{[t]}{2}:~\text{$(s,\{j,j'\},i)\in Q$ for some $s\in I_j\cap I_{j'}$}\right\}.$$ Note that we view each $Q_i$ as a labeled subgraph that preserves the labeling of $G$. Moreover, as $Q$ forms a partial transversal, each $Q_i$ is a simple graph with no multiple edges,  while $G$ could be a multigraph.
nodes.statement_short: Define the subgraphs $Q_i$.

nodes.name: Claim 6.10 block
nodes.statement_short: Claim 6.10 and its proof.

nodes.name: Claim 6.9 proof block
nodes.statement_short: Proof of Claim 6.9, completing the theorem.

nodes.name: Block structure
nodes.statement: By the definition of a partial transversal, $M_Q$ is a $\binom{t-1}{2}k\times \binom{t-1}{2}k$ square matrix with $k$ diagonal blocks, where for each $0\le i\le k-1$, the $(i+1)$-th diagonal block is obtained by removing from $\mathcal{B}_t$ all of the columns that are labeled by the edges of $Q_i$. As $\mathcal{B}_t$ has full row rank, $\det(M_Q)\neq 0$ if and only if each of the $k$ diagonal blocks also has full row rank.
nodes.statement_short: $M_Q$ is block diagonal with blocks $\mathcal{B}_t$ minus the columns of $Q_i$.

nodes.name: Apply Claim 3.5
nodes.statement: By Claim~\ref{claim-property-of-B_t}, the $(i+1)$-th block has full row rank if and only if the labels of the removed columns form an acyclic graph on the vertices $[t]$, namely, $Q_i$ is acyclic.
nodes.statement_short: Each block has full rank iff $Q_i$ is acyclic.

nodes.name: Spanning trees
nodes.statement: Since $k(t-1)$ columns are removed in total, and an acyclic subgraph on $t$ vertices can have at most $t-1$ edges,  $\det(M_Q)\neq 0$ \black{happens if and only if} $Q_i$ is a spanning tree.
nodes.statement_short: Edge counting forces each $Q_i$ to be a spanning tree.

nodes.name: Edge-disjoint
nodes.statement: Moreover, as elements in $Q$ form a partial transversal, we never have $(s,\{j,j,'\},i)$ and $(s,\{j,j'\},i')$ both in $Q$, for $i\neq i'$. It follows that the $Q_i$'s are also pairwise edge-disjoint.
nodes.statement_short: The $Q_i$ are pairwise edge-disjoint.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: \black{Hence, we have $\det(M_Q)\neq 0$ if and only if the $Q_i$'s form pairwise edge-disjoint spanning trees, as desired.}
nodes.statement_short: Conclude the equivalence.

nodes.name: Monomial of transversal
nodes.statement:
With the notation above, it is not hard to check by definition  that for a partial transversal $Q\subseteq U$ with $\det(M_Q)\neq 0$, \begin{align} \prod_{(s,\{j,j'\},i)\in Q}^{} x_s^i=\prod_{s\in S}\prod_{i=0}^{k-1} (x_s^{v_s^{Q_i}})^i=\prod_{s\in S} x_s^{v_s^{(Q_0,\ldots,Q_{k-1})}}=x^{(Q_0,\ldots,Q_{k-1})}.
\end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Each transversal's monomial is $x^{(Q_0,\dots,Q_{k-1})}$.

nodes.name: Sum over packings
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $\det M'$ as a sum over tree packings via Claim 6.10.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement:
It is clear that by the definition of $T_0,\ldots,T_{k-1}$,
in the above summation the monomial $x^{(T_0,\dots,T_{k-1})}$ appears exactly once, and hence appears as a nonvanishing term in the determinant expansion, completing the proof of Claim~\ref{clm:new-1} and thus the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:complete-2}.
nodes.statement_short: The distinguished monomial occurs once, so it survives.

nodes.name: Only-if part
nodes.section: A Perfect Hash Matrices and List-recoverable Codes
nodes.statement_short: Only if: $t$ codewords in small lists give an unseparated set of columns.

nodes.name: If part
nodes.statement: To prove the ``if'' part, assume for contradiction that $M$ is not $t$-perfect hashing. Then, there exist $t$ distinct columns of $M$ (or equivalently, codewords of $\mathcal{C}$), say $c^1,\ldots,c^t$, that cannot be separated by any row of $M$. In other words, for each $1\le i\le n$, $\{c^1_i,\ldots,c^t_i\}$ consists of at most $t-1$ distinct symbols of $[q]$. It is routine to check by definition that $c^1,\ldots,c^t$ violate the list-recoverability of $\mathcal{C}$, and we have arrived at the desired contradiction.
nodes.section: A Perfect Hash Matrices and List-recoverable Codes
nodes.statement_short: If: $t$ unseparated columns violate list-recoverability.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: The results in \cite{CS07,CCV09} look slightly different from Theorem~\ref{thm:conj-weak} and we briefly describe the connection here.
nodes.statement_short: Explain the connection to CS07/CCV09.

nodes.name: Apply cited results
nodes.statement:
Both of the works prove that every $C(\log t)k$-weakly partition-connected hypergraph has $k$ hyperedge-disjoint connected subhypergraphs:\footnote{A hypergraph is connected if, for every two vertices $v$ and $v'$, there is a path $v=v_0,v_1,\dots,v_\ell=v'$ such that, for all $i$, $v_{i-1},v_i$ share a hyperedge.}
the first \cite{CS07} proves an equivalent statement about bipartite Steiner tree packings, and the second \cite{CCV09} proves a more general result about disjoint bases of polymatroids and also improves the constant $C$ in front of the log factor over \cite{CS07}.
nodes.statement_short: Cited results give $k$ hyperedge-disjoint connected subhypergraphs.

nodes.name: Distinguishable subgraph
nodes.statement: Furthermore, it is not difficult to show that, for any hypergraph $H$ with $k$ hyperedge-disjoint connected subhypergraphs $H_0,\dots,H_{k-1}$, any tree assignment of $H$ has a $k$-distinguishable subgraph: briefly, the $k$-distinguishable subgraph $G$ is the union of spanning trees $T_0,\dots,T_{k-1}$ of the tree assignments of $H_0,\dots,H_{k-1}$ that are implied by the tree assignments of $H$, and the spanning trees $T_0,\dots,T_{k-1}$ give the $k$ edge-disjoint spanning trees of $G$ that certify $k$-distinguishability.
nodes.statement_short: Disjoint connected subhypergraphs give a distinguishable subgraph.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence, any $C(\log t)k$-weakly-partition-connected hypergraph has $k$ hyperedge-disjoint connected subhypergraphs and thus is $k$-distinguishable, which is Theorem~\ref{thm:conj-weak}.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude Theorem 6.4.

nodes.name: Use Theorem 6.4
nodes.statement: We point out that Theorem~\ref{thm:conj-weak} can be used to obtain a second proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main-LD} by following the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:complete-2}, which connects hypergraph partitions to intersection matrices and then applies a polynomial method to obtain list decodable Reed--Solomon codes.
nodes.statement_short: Run the proof of Theorem 6.2 with Theorem 6.4.

nodes.name: Rate loss
nodes.statement: The extra $O(\log t)$ factor in the weak-partition-connectivity of Theorem~\ref{thm:conj-weak} appears as an $O(\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon})$ factor loss in the rate of the Reed--Solomon code.
nodes.statement_short: The $\log t$ loss becomes a $\log(1/\varepsilon)$ rate loss.

nodes.name: Omitted details
nodes.statement: Since one proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main-LD} is already given, and the key ideas for this second proof are covered throughout the rest of the paper, we omit the details of this second proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main-LD}.
nodes.statement_short: Details omitted.

nodes.name: Restrict to l=1
nodes.statement:
We give an overview of our proof of Theorem~\ref{list-recover-main}.
For simplicity, let us first assume the input list size $\ell$ equals one, i.e., we restrict to the case of list decoding.
In this case, Theorem~\ref{list-recover-main} states that there exist RS codes of rate $\Omega(\frac{\varepsilon}{\log(1/\varepsilon)+1})$ that are list-decodable from radius $1-\varepsilon$ with list size $O(1/\varepsilon)$.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to list decoding first.

nodes.name: Base on Theorem 3.1
nodes.statement:
As discussed previously, Conjecture~\ref{conjecture} about the nonsingularity of intersection matrices would be enough to establish Theorem~\ref{list-recover-main}, and indeed an even stronger result.
While we do not know if Conjecture~\ref{conjecture} holds in general,  Theorem~\ref{theorem-weaker} states that it holds under an extra condition that $I_i\cap I_{i'}\cap I_{i''}=\emptyset$ for distinct $i,i',i''\in[t]$. Our proof of Theorem~\ref{list-recover-main} is based on this theorem.
nodes.statement_short: The proof rests on Theorem 3.1 instead of Conjecture 1.5.

nodes.name: Naive pruning
nodes.statement:
As Theorem~\ref{theorem-weaker} requires the above extra condition,  which does not hold in general, we cannot simply follow the proof in \cite{shangguan2019combinatorial0} and replace  Conjecture~\ref{conjecture} by Theorem~\ref{theorem-weaker}.
One naive way of fixing this  is removing elements from the sets $I_i$ until the condition $I_i\cap I_{i'}\cap I_{i''}=\emptyset$ for distinct $i,i',i''\in[t]$ is satisfied. Specifically, for each $j\in [n]$ such that there exist more than two sets $I_{i_1}, \dots, I_{i_s}$ containing $j$, we pick two sets (say $I_{i_1}$ and $I_{i_2}$) and remove $j$ from all the other sets. The resulting sets $I'_1,\dots,I'_t$ satisfy the condition $I'_i\cap I'_{i'}\cap I'_{i''}=\emptyset$ for distinct $i,i',i''\in[t]$ and we can now apply Theorem~\ref{theorem-weaker} to conclude that $M_{k,(I'_1,\ldots,I'_t)}$ is nonsingular.
nodes.statement_short: Naive fix: prune elements to kill three-wise intersections.

nodes.name: Loss of naive pruning
nodes.statement:
The problem with this idea, however, is that  ${\rm wt}(I'_{[t]})$ could be much smaller than ${\rm wt}(I_{[t]})$.
Indeed, if a coordinate $j\in [n]$ is simultaneously contained in $s\geq 2$ sets $I_{i_1},\dots,I_{i_s}$, then it is counted $s-1$ times in   ${\rm wt}(I_{[t]})=\sum_{i=1}^t |I_i|-\left|\bigcup_{i=1}^t I_i\right|$ (one for each set $I_{i_u}$, $u=1,\dots,s$, and minus one for $\bigcup_{i=1}^t I_i$). On the other hand, this coordinate is counted only once in ${\rm wt}(I'_{[t]})$ since we have removed it from all but two of the sets $I_{i_u}$.
As $s$ can be as large as $t$, the new weight ${\rm wt}(I'_{[t]})$ can be smaller than ${\rm wt}(I_{[t]})$ by a factor of $t-1=\Omega(1/\varepsilon)$.

As a consequence, implementing this idea directly only yields RS codes of rate $\Omega(\varepsilon^2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Naive pruning loses a factor $t-1$ in weight.

nodes.name: Random sampling
nodes.statement:
To mitigate this problem, we perform a random sampling of the collection $\{I_1,\dots,I_t\}$ before removing elements from $I_i$. Namely, we choose a random subset $J\subseteq [t]$ of some appropriate cardinality to be determined later.
Then,  we remove elements from the sets $I_i$ just like before, but only for $i\in J$, so that the resulting sets $I'_i$ satisfy the condition $I'_i\cap I'_{i'}\cap I'_{i''}=\emptyset$ for distinct $i,i',i''\in J$.
Finally, we apply Theorem~\ref{theorem-weaker} to conclude that  the $|J|$-wise intersection matrix $M_{k,(I'_i)_{i\in J}}$ is nonsingular, which can still be used to prove the list-decodability of the RS code.

The advantage of replacing $[t]$ by the random sample $J\subseteq [t]$ is that the condition ${\rm wt}(I'_{[t]})\geq (t-1)k$
is replaced by ${\rm wt}(I'_{J})\geq (|J|-1)k$. It turns out that the condition $I_i'\cap I_{i'}'\cap I_{i''}'=\emptyset$ for distinct $i,i',i''\in J$ is easier to satisfy since  $|J|$ may be much smaller than $t$.
Consequently, we are able to show that there exist RS codes of rate $\Omega(\frac{\varepsilon}{\log(1/\varepsilon)+1})$ using this improved method.
nodes.statement_short: Randomly sample $J$ before pruning.

nodes.name: Bucketing
nodes.statement:
Finally, we explain how to choose the cardinality of the sample $J$.
Let $j\in [n]$ and denote by $s_j$ the number of sets among $I_1,\dots, I_t$ that contain  $j$.
Then for the index $j$, we choose $|J|=\Theta(t/s_j)$ for our purpose.
However, the number $s_j$ may vary  when $j$ ranges over $[n]$, meaning that there may not be a single choice of $|J|$ that works best for all $j\in [n]$ simultaneously.

We solve this problem using the following trick: Create a logarithmic number of ``buckets'' and put $j\in [n]$ in the $i$-th bucket if $2^{i-1} \leq s_j<2^i$. Then choose $|J|$ according to the heaviest bucket. Here, we lose a factor of $O(\log(1/\varepsilon)+1)$ in the rate because there are about $\log L = O(\log(1/\varepsilon)+1)$ buckets.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $|J|$ via logarithmically many buckets.

nodes.name: List recovery
nodes.statement:
\paragraph{Generalization to list recovery.} In the case of list decoding, we choose each set $I_i$ to be the subset of coordinates where a codeword $c_i$ and the received word $y$ agree.  In the more general setting of list recovery, each $I_i$ is the subset of $j\in [n]$ where $j$-th coordinate of $c_i$ belongs to a certain set $S_j\subseteq \mathbb{F}_q$ of size $\ell$.
So the $j$-th coordinate of $c_i$ may take at most $\ell$ possible values, which may be thought of as $\ell$ different ``colors."


One way of extending our proof to list recovery is choosing subsets $I'_1\subseteq I_1,\dots,I'_t\subseteq I_t$ that come from coordinates of codewords with the same color, where the colors are picked such that ${\rm wt}(I'_{[t]})={\rm wt}(I'_1,\dots, I'_t)$ is maximized. Then we proceed as in the case of list decoding.
It is not hard to show that this yields RS codes of rate $\Omega(\frac{\varepsilon}{\ell(\log(1/\varepsilon)+1)})$ which are list-recoverable from radius $1-\varepsilon$ with input list size $\ell$ and output list size $O(\ell/\varepsilon)$.

With a more careful analysis, we show that we can achieve a better rate  $\Omega(\frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{\ell}(\log(1/\varepsilon)+1)})$, as stated by Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
Our analysis is inspired by \cite{LP20} which proved a similar result on the list-recoverability of randomly punctured
codes with a different setting of parameters.
nodes.statement_short: Extend to list recovery with colors, gaining $\sqrt{\ell}$.
